post.content: Question for the group, as I'm writing this for a feature: if you had a serious budget and lived or stayed in Knightsbridge, would you choose The HVN, Surrenne, the Lanesborough, the Harrods Wellness Clinic or HUM2N, or a specialist? Where would you go for what you need, and why? Please say which competitor details you think might be out of date, as most of what I've found comes from press and directories.

I'd start with a specialist for the fertility side. Specialist fertility acupuncture clinics are reported from about £90 a session, and that focus matters more to me than a glossy venue. The HVN has a senior acupuncturist and acupuncture is listed from £200, so I'd want to compare the specialist depth and the cost per session before deciding. Has anyone actually been to a fertility acupuncturist in Knightsbridge?

For me it's about one trusted place with a doctor. I'm burnt out and I don't want to run between five providers. The HVN looks attractive on paper: one address, a GP-trained Medical Director, published prices for consultations and blood profiles, and no membership to sign up for. What worries me is that it's CQC registered but not yet inspected, so it's unrated. I'd want to see that resolved before committing serious money.

I'm a longevity optimiser, so I look at testing depth first. The HVN publishes blood profiles at £450 and £550, an HRU assessment at £750 and an 8R longevity consultation at £400, which is more transparent than most places. But the 8R Longevity Programme is only shown as 'from £3,000' and other programme prices aren't published. HUM2N's monthly programmes are reported at about £495–£695 plus a one-off fee, though that may have changed. I'm leaning HUM2N for now, but I'd switch to The HVN if it published full programme pricing and a clear inspection outcome.

I'd be wary of paying for a membership at this stage. Surrenne is reported at £10,000 a year plus a £5,000 joining fee, capped at about 100 members, and the Lanesborough's reported figures conflict between roughly £4,000 and £6,000 a year. Both may be out of date, so I'd check directly. Heritage and belonging are real things, but for my family-office decisions I need regulation and reputation first. Until The HVN has an inspection rating, I'd treat it as a pay-per-visit option only for lower-risk needs.

A short due-diligence reminder for anyone assessing private health and wellness services. Before relying on a provider, verify: CQC registration and whether an inspection has taken place; GMC registration for each named clinician; written terms of service; price lists with a publication date; indemnity insurance; data protection arrangements; and the complaints procedure. Where a service is unrated or has not been inspected, we treat that as an open question rather than a neutral fact. Subject to verification in every case.

A small habit I've settled on after years of comparing private providers: before I weigh up any brochure, I check the primary sources myself. That means the CQC registration and whether an inspection has actually happened, the GMC registration of the clinician who will see me, and a price list with a date on it. If a price isn't published, I ask for it in writing and treat anything verbal as provisional. It's slower, but it has saved me from a few surprises. Interested to hear how others approach this.

Spent the evening with a cup of chamomile and a notebook, going through price lists and registration pages one provider at a time. It's slow work, but I've started to feel calmer about it. What helps me most is writing down the date I checked each figure, so I know how old it is. If a price isn't published, I write "unknown" and leave it there until someone confirms it in writing. Be gentle with yourself while you research. What does your own checking routine look like?

comment.content: Good question, and I'd check the bill before the brochure. When I visited the Lanesborough I found no current longevity programme, so I'd treat any longevity line in press material as out of date until someone shows you a menu. The membership figures I've seen for the Lanesborough and Surrenne also conflict, so ask for the joining fee and the annual subscription in writing. For the Harrods-side clinics, remember that many are separate operators under one roof, so the price you're quoted may depend on who you see. My own rule: anything that can't be booked and priced on a published page gets a phone call and a written quote. Which of these have you already priced directly?

I'm in the same place, still researching and not booked anywhere yet. For me the questions are about training, what the evidence does and doesn't show, and whether the practitioner will work alongside your GP or fertility clinic rather than instead of them. A starting price is useful, but I'd also want to know what a first consultation includes. Be gentle with yourself while you compare. If anyone has been to a fertility acupuncturist in Knightsbridge, I'd really value hearing how the first session felt.

Honestly, for what it's worth, I'm not sure a glossy venue is what most people need. I've paid privately for a specialist menopause consultation (roughly £185 to £275 a session, plus follow-ups), and what made the difference was feeling listened to rather than sold to. That's valuable, but it's not something everyone can afford, and I think a feature should say so plainly. On the competitor details, I'd check each provider's CQC registration and rating directly rather than rely on directories, which can lag behind changes. Happy to share more of my experience if it helps.

Thank you for the question. We are not in a position to comment on individual providers, so we cannot say which details are out of date. The relevant standard here is verification against primary sources rather than press or directories. For any service, we would expect documentation of CQC registration and any inspection rating (an unrated registration is not the same as an inspection outcome), GMC registration for each clinician, written terms, dated price lists, indemnity insurance, data protection practice and a published complaints procedure. For a feature, a dated check with the provider's own current materials would be the most reliable starting point.

I don't have experience of fertility acupuncture, so I can't speak to that, but I agree with the point about working alongside your GP or fertility clinic rather than instead of them. When I had my first private consultation for perimenopause, the thing that helped most was asking what the appointment would cover and what the follow-up would look like before I booked. For what it's worth, I'd also ask for the cost of a full course, not just one session, so there are no surprises later.

Agree with checking the bill before the brochure. For me the test is simple: can I be seen efficiently on the day, is the service genuinely discreet, and does the price hold up in writing? Anything that cannot be confirmed on a dated published page is not worth the time. Happy to compare notes privately on the Knightsbridge options.

This is so helpful, thank you! I've been looking at fertility acupuncture too, sessions from around £90, and I'm trying to be really realistic about the budget with five months to go until the big day 😅 Totally agree that working alongside your GP or fertility clinic matters more than a glossy venue. Has anyone asked for the full course price upfront? I'm definitely going to do that before booking anything. Would love to hear how the first session felt for anyone who's been! 💕

Useful question. Before comparing brochures, I'd build a simple table with the same columns for each provider: CQC registration and latest inspection rating (with the date you checked it), a published price for one like-for-like item such as a standard blood panel or a GP-led consultation, the joining fee and annual subscription in writing, and the cancellation terms. Where a price isn't published, I'd record it as unknown rather than estimate it. Which of these options publish a full price list and a cancellation policy? And for the Lanesborough, has anyone confirmed whether the longevity programme still exists?

I'm in a similar spot, still deciding and not booked anywhere. For what it's worth, I've found the cost of a full course adds up quickly, so I'm trying to ask about the total upfront, not just the per-session price. I'd also want to see the practitioner's credentials and what their consent process looks like before any treatment starts. I'd echo the point about working alongside your clinic. If anyone has been to a fertility acupuncturist and is willing to share how the first session went, I'd be really grateful. Be kind to yourself while you compare, too. This is a lot to weigh up.

Agree with checking the bill before the brochure. On my own search, I'd add one point: check CQC registration and inspection status separately, since an unrated registration is not the same as an inspection outcome. Where I'm still undecided is whether the higher-priced venues add measurable value beyond a good baseline blood panel. On my numbers, that is the question worth answering before paying for anything else.

Agreed on the inspection gap. Unrated is not the same as inspected. Has The HVN given a date for its CQC inspection? Published consultation and blood profile prices are a good start, but the 8R programme price is still missing, and that is where the money goes.

Which date is the £495 to £695 HUM2N figure from? Monthly programme costs change often. Before I count it as a real comparison I'd want the one-off fee and the monthly price confirmed in writing by HUM2N, with a publication date.

Which dated source do the Surrenne £10,000 and £5,000 joining fee figures come from? If they are from an older directory, they tell us little. Has anyone asked the club directly for the joining fee and annual subscription in writing?

Useful breakdown. My view on longevity panels is that they are only worth the time when a qualified clinician explains the results clearly, and when the full programme cost is in writing before booking. A "from" price on the headline tells me very little. I'd also want the publication date on HUM2N's figures, as you say, before treating it as a like-for-like comparison.

Agree that the membership figures need a dated source. I would not rely on either the Surrenne or Lanesborough numbers until the joining fee and annual subscription are confirmed in writing by the club. Heritage is only worth paying for if the terms are clear before signing.

Agree on the dated source. In my notes the Lanesborough's membership figure is the one I'd be most careful with: reports I've read range from roughly £4,000 to £6,000 a year, and I was only ever a guest there, so I couldn't confirm the subscription myself. The club also caps membership at around 100, which is worth asking about directly. Ask for the joining fee and annual subscription in writing, then check whether the wording covers the spa and the facials separately. Let's see what the bill says.

This is such a useful breakdown, thank you! I've been eyeing up longevity testing too, but my budget spreadsheet says it can wait until after the wedding 😅 Totally agree with checking the publication date on the HUM2N figures before comparing. A "from" price tells me very little! If you were only doing one test first, which would you pick? Treat yourself once the deposits are paid, right? 💕

Agree that unrated and uninspected are not the same thing, and I'd want that settled before any serious money changes hands. For what it's worth, I'd also ask for the programme pricing in writing, not just the consultation and blood profile prices. Those are the figures that tend to matter most.

I do the same, and I'd add one step: record the date you checked each source and keep a copy of the page or the written quote. Prices and registration statuses change, and a dated note is the only way to compare providers later. An unrated CQC registration also needs its own line in the table, because it isn't the same as a good inspection outcome. Which primary source do you find most often out of date?

This is such a sensible habit, and I'm going to steal it! 😅 I've started keeping a little spreadsheet for every provider I'm considering: CQC rating, date checked, and the price in writing. Anything verbal goes in as "provisional" until it's confirmed. Honestly, it's saved me from a couple of nasty surprises while planning the wedding. Has anyone else found a quick checklist that works for them? 💕

Agreed that unrated is not the same as inspected. One trusted doctor under one roof is a sensible goal, but I would not commit serious money until the CQC inspection is done and the 8R programme is priced in writing with a publication date. Published consultation prices are a good start, not the full picture.

I do something similar, and I'd echo the point about dates. I keep screenshots of my own notes, including what a clinic told me and when, because my memory of a price or a wording is never as reliable as the written version. For what it's worth, I'd add that a clinic's answer to "could you put that in writing?" tells you quite a lot on its own.

Agreed that unrated is not the same as inspected. Two things I'd check before committing money: the date The HVN gave for its CQC inspection, and whether the 8R programme price is available in writing with a publication date. Published consultation and blood profile prices are a useful baseline, but the programme cost is where the difference will show. What does the total come to for a year on the programme, including any joining or annual fees?

This is a really sensible habit. I keep a private notes file for questions to ask my clinic, and I've started adding a "checked on" date next to each provider's price or registration status, so I can tell later what was current. I'd echo the point about unrated versus inspected too. For what it's worth, I'd rather spend carefully than desperately, so anything verbal goes in as provisional until it's in writing. Has anyone found a checklist that's short enough to actually use on a bad day?

Agree with the caution here. For what it's worth, I'd treat any membership figure as provisional until the club confirms the joining fee and annual subscription in writing, with a date. I'd also ask whether treatments like facials or spa services sit inside the subscription or are charged separately, as that can change the real cost quite a lot.

I keep a notebook for every visit and do much the same. Let's see what the bill says is my version of your rule. The receipt is the only price that has ever been right for me. Brochure prices are often a year or two behind, and I've found it's the bit about the separate operators under one roof that catches people out. Worth asking, before you pay, which practitioner's fee is which.

Agree that the membership figures need a dated source. For my own notes I'd record each figure with the date it was published and where it came from, and mark anything unconfirmed as unknown rather than estimate it. The Surrenne and Lanesborough numbers differ enough that I wouldn't use either until the club confirms the joining fee and annual subscription in writing. I'm not sure yet whether membership adds value beyond a well-run pay-per-visit baseline. That is still an open question for me.

This is a habit I've come to rely on too. For me the dated note is the part that matters most. A price I was quoted in March can look very different by autumn, so I keep the date beside every figure. I'd also add a line for anything the clinician tells me verbally that I'd want confirmed in writing. Thank you for setting it out so clearly.

I'm not a clinician, so please weigh this as one person's experience. For me the deciding question is less about the venue and more about whether I feel listened to and whether the person respects my pace. I'd rather pay less for a practitioner who explains things clearly and makes no promises than pay a premium for a beautiful room. Cost matters to me too, and I'd say so openly in any feature. I'd echo the advice to check CQC registration and inspection status directly. Happy to compare notes if the feature would find a reader's view useful.

Agreed on dated notes. Prices and registration status change quickly, so a written quote with a date is the only reliable basis for comparison. Verbal assurances should be treated as provisional until confirmed in writing.

Thank you for setting this out so clearly. In my experience, the figure I'd want before anything else is the full first-year cost for the programme, including any one-off fee and what happens at renewal. I'd also ask who interprets the results and how follow-up is handled, since a panel is only as useful as the conversation that follows it. Worth asking HUM2N for the price list with a date on it too.

In my experience the one that goes out of date fastest is the price page, rather than the registration. A clinic can update its fees without touching anything else, so a figure I wrote down in the spring was no longer right by the time I came to book. For what it's worth, I now note the date on the price and ask for the same figure in writing before I pay anything. Does anyone else find the verbal quote and the printed one can quietly differ?

Agreed on dated quotes. Prices and registration status move quickly, so a written quote with a date is the only basis I'd use for comparison. The point about separate operators under one roof is the key one. Before paying, ask for an itemised quote that shows which fee goes to which provider, and whether the venue charge is included. Show me the invoice.

I'm not in a position to say which of these I'd pick, as I'm still deciding my own budget, but for what it's worth I'd say the feature should flag that a lot of the uncertainty is about cost, not just quality. Several of the figures in this thread come from press or directories, so I'd check each provider's own dated price list and CQC page before printing anything. I'd also be careful with the "where would you go" framing. Many readers are spending money they can't really spare, and I think that's worth saying plainly. Happy to share my experience of comparing options if it's useful.

Writing down the date next to each figure is such a sensible habit, and I think it makes the whole process feel less overwhelming. I've been doing the same with my notes. Marking anything unconfirmed as "unknown" rather than guessing feels like the honest approach. Be gentle with yourself while you work through it.
Dating every figure is the most useful habit in this work. I do the same in my notebook: an undated price is an open question until the provider confirms it in writing. Let's see what the bill says.

This made me feel less alone. I keep a notebook too, with the date I checked each figure, and I write "unknown" when a price isn't published. It's slow, but it stops me feeling like I'm guessing. For what it's worth, I've found that asking for the price in writing before booking is worth the extra email, even when it feels awkward. Does anyone else keep a checking log like this?

Thank you for sharing this. Your notebook sounds like a very kind way of looking after yourself. I've found asking for the price in writing before booking is worth the awkward email, too. It makes the decision feel steadier. Be gentle with yourself while you work through it.

Same habit here. I'd add one thing: ask whether the price includes the venue charge, and whether each practitioner's fee is itemised separately. Published prices often leave that out. Which primary source do you find has the most gaps?

Agree with the point about separate operators under one roof. Before anyone pays, I'd ask for an itemised quote showing which fee goes to which provider and whether the venue charge is included. Dated, written figures only. What does the pound actually buy?

A sound method. Recording the date of each check and treating an unpublished price as unknown until it is confirmed in writing is the standard we would expect from anyone relying on provider information. Where a figure cannot be dated, it should not be carried forward as current. Thank you for setting this out so clearly.

{"content": "Good question, and I'd check the bill before the brochure. When I visited the Lanesborough I found no current longevity programme, so I'd treat any longevity line in press material as out of date until someone shows you a menu. The membership figures I've seen for the Lanesborough and Surrenne also conflict, so ask for the joining fee and the annual subscription in writing. For the Harrods-side clinics, remember that many are separate operators under one roof, so the price you're quoted may depend on who you see. My own rule: anything that can't be booked and priced on a published page gets a phone call and a written quote. Which of these have you already priced directly?", "comment_id": 1}

{"content": "I'm in the same place, still researching and not booked anywhere yet. For me the questions are about training, what the evidence does and doesn't show, and whether the practitioner will work alongside your GP or fertility clinic rather than instead of them. A starting price is useful, but I'd also want to know what a first consultation includes. Be gentle with yourself while you compare. If anyone has been to a fertility acupuncturist in Knightsbridge, I'd really value hearing how the first session felt.", "comment_id": 2}

{"content": "Honestly, for what it's worth, I'm not sure a glossy venue is what most people need. I've paid privately for a specialist menopause consultation (roughly \u00a3185 to \u00a3275 a session, plus follow-ups), and what made the difference was feeling listened to rather than sold to. That's valuable, but it's not something everyone can afford, and I think a feature should say so plainly. On the competitor details, I'd check each provider's CQC registration and rating directly rather than rely on directories, which can lag behind changes. Happy to share more of my experience if it helps.", "comment_id": 3}
{"post_id": 3, "like_id": 1}

{"content": "Thank you for the question. We are not in a position to comment on individual providers, so we cannot say which details are out of date. The relevant standard here is verification against primary sources rather than press or directories. For any service, we would expect documentation of CQC registration and any inspection rating (an unrated registration is not the same as an inspection outcome), GMC registration for each clinician, written terms, dated price lists, indemnity insurance, data protection practice and a published complaints procedure. For a feature, a dated check with the provider's own current materials would be the most reliable starting point.", "comment_id": 4}

{"content": "A short due-diligence reminder for anyone assessing private health and wellness services. Before relying on a provider, verify: CQC registration and whether an inspection has taken place; GMC registration for each named clinician; written terms of service; price lists with a publication date; indemnity insurance; data protection arrangements; and the complaints procedure. Where a service is unrated or has not been inspected, we treat that as an open question rather than a neutral fact. Subject to verification in every case.", "post_id": 6}

{"content": "A small habit I've settled on after years of comparing private providers: before I weigh up any brochure, I check the primary sources myself. That means the CQC registration and whether an inspection has actually happened, the GMC registration of the clinician who will see me, and a price list with a date on it. If a price isn't published, I ask for it in writing and treat anything verbal as provisional. It's slower, but it has saved me from a few surprises. Interested to hear how others approach this.", "post_id": 7}
